claim: AC 150/5300-13B defines the RPZ for a precision instrument runway with visibility minimums below 3/4-mile as 2,500 feet long, 1,000 feet inner width, 1,750 feet outer width, beginning 200 feet beyond the runway end.
supporting_excerpt: The RPZ dimension for a particular runway end is a function of the type of aircraft and approach visibility minimum associated with that runway end. The RPZ begins 200 feet beyond the end of the area usable for takeoff or landing.
caveat: AC is advisory guidance, not a binding regulation under 14 CFR. However, FAA uses deviations as evidence of grant assurance violations.

claim: RPZ land use: sponsors should take appropriate measures to protect against, remove, or mitigate land uses that introduce incompatible development within RPZs; a data center is not among any listed compatible use.
source_title: AC 150/5190-4B, Airport Land Use Compatibility Planning, September 2022
page_or_section: Section 2 and RPZ Land Use guidance
supporting_excerpt: Sponsors should take appropriate measures to protect against, remove, or mitigate land uses that introduce incompatible development within RPZs. The FAA expects the airport sponsor to take active steps to prevent or mitigate proposed incompatible land uses.
caveat: Advisory circular; not legally binding. But FAA uses it as the standard against which grant assurance compliance is measured.

claim: Grant Assurance 20 (Hazard Removal and Mitigation) requires sponsors to take appropriate action to assure that terminal airspace required for instrument and visual operations is adequately cleared and protected by removing, lowering, lighting, marking, or otherwise mitigating hazards.
supporting_excerpt: Airport sponsors will take appropriate action to assure that such terminal airspace as is required to protect instrument and visual operations to the airport will be adequately cleared and protected.
airport_or_entity: All AIP grant recipients including MWAA
caveat: Contractual obligation binding on MWAA. Enforcement via 14 CFR Part 16. Duration: 20 years from most recent grant.

claim: Grant Assurance 21 (Compatible Land Use) requires the airport sponsor to take appropriate action to restrict incompatible land uses around the airport.
supporting_excerpt: The sponsor will take appropriate action to restrict incompatible land uses around the airport and to protect approaches by removing, lowering, lighting, or marking hazards.
airport_or_entity: All AIP grant recipients including MWAA
caveat: Interpretation of 'incompatible' is FAA-defined. FAA expects affirmative sponsorship action, not merely passive non-approval.

claim: Grant Assurance 29 (Airport Layout Plan) requires the sponsor to keep an up-to-date ALP on file with the FAA and not permit changes to the airport inconsistent with it without FAA approval.
source_title: FAA Airport Sponsor Assurances (April 2025); FAA Federal Register Update April 25 2025
source_type: FAA Grant Assurance (contractual obligation); Federal Register
supporting_excerpt: The sponsor must keep an up-to-date Airport Layout Plan on file with the FAA and must not make or permit changes to the airport that are inconsistent with it without FAA approval.
airport_or_entity: All AIP grant recipients including MWAA
caveat: Updated April 2025 to conform to FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 Section 743; FAA review authority now limited to three specific criteria.

claim: 14 CFR Part 77 Section 77.9 requires notice to FAA for any construction or alteration exceeding the 100:1 imaginary surface within 20,000 feet of an airport with instrument approaches, triggering mandatory aeronautical study via Form 7460-1.
source_title: 14 CFR Part 77, Safe Efficient Use and Preservation of the Navigable Airspace
supporting_excerpt: Any construction or alteration that exceeds an imaginary surface extending outward and upward at a 100 to 1 slope for a horizontal distance of 20,000 ft. requires notice. The FAA will determine whether the effect of proposed construction or alteration is a hazard to air navigation.
airport_or_entity: All construction near public-use airports with instrument approaches
caveat: This is a binding federal regulation, not advisory. Non-compliance is not curable by AIP agreement. Aeronautical study timeline up to 120 days.

claim: FAA aeronautical study can result in a Determination of Hazard that independently blocks construction without reference to grant assurances. Determinations of No Hazard expire 18 months unless extended.
source_title: 14 CFR Part 77, Subpart D — Aeronautical Studies and Determinations
supporting_excerpt: FAA issues Hazard or No Hazard determinations. Determinations of No Hazard expire 18 months unless extended or revised.
airport_or_entity: All proposed construction requiring Part 77 notice
caveat: A Hazard Determination can be appealed to FAA headquarters under 77.37 but is rarely reversed without project redesign.

claim: FAA AIM Section 7-6-16 warns that thermal plume turbulence from cooling towers can extend more than 1,000 feet above stack height and that results of encountering a plume may include airframe damage, aircraft upset, and engine damage/failure, with hazards most critical in approach and departure corridors.
source_title: Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM), Section 7-6-16, Avoid Flight in the Vicinity of Exhaust Plumes
supporting_excerpt: Results of encountering a plume may include airframe damage, aircraft upset, and/or engine damage/failure. These hazards are most critical during low altitude flight in calm and cold air, especially in and around approach and departure corridors or airport traffic areas. Studies predict that the significant turbulent effects of an exhaust plume can extend to heights of over 1,000 feet above the height of the top of the stack or cooling tower.
airport_or_entity: All airport approach and departure corridors
caveat: AIM is guidance to pilots, not a regulatory prohibition on siting. However, it is the FAA's published safety determination and would be cited in any aeronautical study for a cooling-tower-equipped facility near an approach corridor.

claim: FAA September 24, 2015 Technical Guidance Assessment Tool memorandum explicitly states that thermal exhaust plumes in the vicinity of airports are incompatible with airport operations and may pose unique hazards to aircraft in critical phases of flight.
source_title: FAA Technical Guidance — Assessment Tool for Evaluation of Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact on Airport Operations
supporting_excerpt: The FAA has determined that thermal exhaust plumes in the vicinity of airports are incompatible with airport operations and may pose unique hazards to aircraft in critical phases of flight, particularly during takeoff, landing and within the pattern.
airport_or_entity: All airports with power plants, cooling towers, or industrial facilities in vicinity
caveat: Memorandum, not a formal AC or rulemaking. But constitutes FAA's institutional position and would inform any aeronautical study of a data center cooling system.

claim: FAA Order 6750.16E establishes that structures within 15 degrees of extended centerline up to 1 NM from the approach end must be studied for ILS signal interference, and explicitly states that placing an object outside the critical area does not guarantee non-interference with the ILS signal in space.
source_title: FAA Order 6750.16E, Siting Criteria for Instrument Landing Systems
source_type: FAA Order (internal FAA directive, binding on FAA Technical Operations)
page_or_section: ILS Critical Area and Siting Requirements
supporting_excerpt: Large mass structures of any type within plus/minus 15 degrees of extended centerline up to 1 NM from the approach end of the runway must be studied carefully. Placing an object outside the critical area does not guarantee non-interference with the ILS signal in space.
caveat: FAA Order binds FAA Technical Operations personnel; it does not directly bind airport sponsors. But FAA Tech Ops can independently require ILS signal analysis and refuse to certify Cat II/III approaches if interference is detected.

claim: AC 150/5200-33C recommends that new stormwater management facilities within 10,000 feet of runways serving turbine-powered aircraft be designed and operated so as not to create above-ground standing water.
source_title: AC 150/5200-33C, Hazardous Wildlife Attractants on or Near Airports
page_or_section: Section on Stormwater Management Facility Design
supporting_excerpt: New storm water management facilities located within 10,000 feet of runways serving turbine-powered aircraft should be designed and operated so as not to create above-ground standing water. Detention basins should remain totally dry between rainfalls.
airport_or_entity: All airports with turbine operations (all IAD runways qualify)
caveat: Advisory circular, not binding regulation. However, data center cooling typically requires persistent water features. Non-compliance with this guidance would be cited in FAA review.

claim: FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 Section 743 limits FAA ALP approval authority to three criteria: materially impacting aviation safety, adversely affecting safety of people or property from aircraft operations, or adversely affecting value of prior federal investments.
source_title: FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Section 743; FAA October 3 2024 ALP Preliminary Instructions Memorandum
supporting_excerpt: FAA retains authority to review and approve only those ALP changes that (1) materially impact the safe and efficient operation of aircraft, (2) adversely affect the safety of people or property on the ground as a result of aircraft operations, or (3) adversely affect the value of prior Federal investments to a significant extent.
caveat: The new NOI process gives FAA 45 days to assert authority. For approach-surface development, all three criteria are implicated; FAA will assert authority within the 45-day window.

claim: FAA December 2023 Federal Register policy (88 FR 85474, effective January 8, 2024) requires FAA consent for land use changes on federally acquired or conveyed airport land, and categorizes non-aeronautical uses (warehouses, hotels) separately from aeronautical uses; IAD sits on federally acquired land.
source_title: FAA Federal Register Policy — Processing Land Use Changes on Federally Acquired or Federally Conveyed Airport Land
supporting_excerpt: The FAA evaluates the primary purpose of the requested use to determine if it is aeronautical, airport purpose, mixed-use, or non-aeronautical. Non-aeronautical uses do not carry the priority protection of aeronautical uses.
airport_or_entity: All airports on federally acquired or conveyed land
caveat: Policy, not rulemaking. But binding on FAA practice. Does not override Grant Assurance 20/21 approach protection requirements.

claim: Watsonville Municipal Airport (2026): court ruled city violated state aeronautical law by approving development within airport safety zones without complying with mandatory airport safety standards; injunction blocks future approvals until general plan updated.
source_title: Court Hands Victory to Watsonville Pilots in Airport Land-Use Dispute, General Aviation News
source_type: Court Decision (Santa Cruz County Superior Court, Feb. 3, 2026)
supporting_excerpt: In a 24-page decision issued February 3, 2026, Santa Cruz County Superior Court Judge Timothy Schmal ruled in favor of the Watsonville Pilots Association, finding that the city unlawfully approved development projects near Watsonville Municipal Airport without complying with state aeronautical law and prior court orders.
caveat: State court ruling under California State Aeronautics Act, not federal grant assurance law. Analogous principle: approach-surface protection requirements cannot be waived by local/sponsor board action without regulatory compliance.

claim: Puente Power Project (CEC Docket 15-AFC-01): FAA aeronautical study found cooling tower thermal plumes would pose significant hazard to aircraft on departure climbing between 1,000 and 3,000 feet; project required siting modifications before CEC approval.
source_title: California Energy Commission Docket 15-AFC-01, Puente Power Project
page_or_section: FAA aeronautical study findings within CEC docket
supporting_excerpt: The FAA's analysis of departure tracks indicated that the resulting thermal plume could pose a significant hazard to small and medium-sized aircraft on departure from Runways 27 and 21 as they make departure turns very near or over the alternative site while climbing between 1,000 and 3,000 feet.
airport_or_entity: Long Beach Airport (LGB), California; Puente Power Project
caveat: California Energy Commission proceeding, not FAA formal rulemaking. Closest documented precedent for data center cooling tower plume impact on approach/departure corridors. Same thermal physics apply.

claim: MWAA is actively soliciting data center development on three IAD parcels with FAA-dependent height limits of 80-200 feet; height limits cited acknowledge Part 77 review is already anticipated by MWAA planning.
source_title: MWAA IAD Data Center Development Opportunity — Real Estate Department
page_or_section: Site descriptions for Moran Road, Route 267, and Pacific Boulevard parcels
supporting_excerpt: Height capacity: approximately 80-160 feet (FAA-dependent) [Moran Road site]; approximately 140-200 feet (FAA-dependent) [Route 267 site]; approximately 120-140 feet (FAA-dependent) [Pacific Boulevard site].
airport_or_entity: IAD Washington Dulles International Airport / MWAA
caveat: These three solicitation parcels appear to be north of the airport, outside primary approach corridors. The planning memo under review concerns a separate proposed site within approach/departure surfaces. The distinction is the operative regulatory fact.

claim: IAD Runway 19R is equipped with ALSF-2 approach lighting (highest category system) indicating Cat II/III ILS operations; this runway serves Category C and D aircraft at approach speeds above 121 knots.
source_title: KIAD ILS RWY 19C (CAT II-III) Instrument Approach Procedure — FlightAware
source_type: FAA Instrument Approach Procedure Chart (via FlightAware)
page_or_section: Approach chart header and lighting notation
supporting_excerpt: Runway 19R at Washington Dulles International Airport is equipped with ALSF-2 approach lighting and serves Cat II/III ILS operations.
airport_or_entity: IAD Washington Dulles International Airport, Runway 19R
caveat: ALSF-2 is the highest-category approach lighting system; its presence confirms Cat II/III operations which require the most stringent ILS signal protection standards under FAA Order 6750.16E.

claim: Grant assurance enforcement through 14 CFR Part 16 proceedings can result in orders requiring corrective action, designation on the Airport Noncompliance List, and denial of future AIP grants; violation of airport revenue provisions carries a penalty of double the illegal diversion plus interest.
source_title: 14 CFR Part 16, Rules of Practice for Federally-Assisted Airport Enforcement Proceedings
page_or_section: 14 CFR Part 16 general provisions; 49 U.S.C. 46301 (penalty provisions)
supporting_excerpt: Part 16 proceedings are administrative adjudications designed to bring airports back into compliance. Failure to comply will land the airport on the Airport Noncompliance List and subject the sponsor to denial of future funding and potential grant repayment.
caveat: Part 16 requires a complainant (airline, pilot association, or FAA). FAA can also initiate compliance actions under 14 CFR Part 13 informally. For MWAA, noncompliance list placement would affect all pending AIP grants including CIP projects.

claim: FAA's September 19, 2022 Policy Guidance on Approach and Departure Surface Protection requires FAA regional and district office consultation when airport projects result in specific land uses within RPZs, including fuel storage, hazardous materials, and aboveground utilities.
source_title: FAA Policy Guidance: Approach and Departure Surface Protection
supporting_excerpt: FAA Regional Office and Airports District Office personnel are required to consult with the National Airport Planning and Environmental Division whenever an airport project would result in specific land uses being located within the RPZ, including recreational uses, transportation facilities, fuel storage facilities, hazardous materials storage, and aboveground utilities.
caveat: Policy guidance, not rulemaking. But imposes mandatory FAA headquarters consultation requirement for RPZ land uses. Data centers are not listed as compatible uses; they are large industrial facilities with electronic and thermal emissions analogous to prohibited categories.
